prize_parts.citation: for methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, which made it possible to measure markups, mergers and policy effects empirically

statement.case_for: The random-coefficients demand framework of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes solved a concrete identification problem: price endogeneity combined with realistic substitution patterns across products. That made it possible to recover demand, markups and counterfactual policy effects from market-level data. It did more than introduce a tool. It supplied an explanatory framework that disciplines the data, which is the combination I value (new empirical capacity plus a framework that explains). Three decades of use in merger review, regulation, auctions, trade, health and environmental economics show the contribution is durable and used beyond its home field. The three-name core is compact and traceable to specific papers (Berry 1994; Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995), and Pakes's dynamic-industry work adds independent foundational weight. Structural industrial organisation has had no recent recognition. My ranking rests on these common criteria of scientific importance, attribution clarity and maturity, and not on field proximity. The work is outside my own field of labour and crime economics.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the credit is cut. Bresnahan and Reiss (empirical entry and market structure) and Benkard and Levin (dynamic estimation) are credited on the ballot but left out by the three-name limit. The demand-estimation core and the dynamic-games estimation line are also not identical achievements, so a citation centred on BLP gives less weight to the dynamic work. In addition, the results depend on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, and critics ask how sensitive counterfactuals are to them. Finally, this ballot has less support across colleagues than the macro-finance and labour candidates. I do not treat that as evidence about merit, but it means the cross-field significance has to be argued explicitly.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B047 first and sees BLP plus Ericson-Pakes as having made industrial organisation quantitative and policy-relevant. He concedes that the three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Levin and Benkard, and that some credit may belong to the wider structural-IO tradition.
responses.response: I agree on the core, and I share the concern about the broader tradition. After reading the openings I think it argues for a narrow, paper-anchored citation, not a broad 'structural IO' one. A citation tied to demand estimation with endogenous prices keeps the attribution defensible. The Bresnahan-Reiss entry work and the dynamic-games estimation line are real contributions, but they are separable achievements. Including them would turn a clean trio into a contested five- or seven-person award.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B047 second and calls the BLP attribution clean. He warns that structural IO's reliance on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions may temper enthusiasm. He ranks the Kiyotaki-Moore and financial-accelerator macro-finance work first on influence, theory and post-2008 vindication.
responses.response: The assumption-dependence point is fair and I do not dismiss it. The distinction I would draw is that BLP's identifying assumptions are explicit, and applied users routinely probe them with sensitivity analysis and with validation against natural experiments and merger retrospectives. On B006, his argument that the macro-finance mechanisms are durable and tested by the crisis is strong. Where I differ is on how much the empirical identification of collateral channels, which he, Stromberg and others also flag as mixed, should count against it relative to the more clearly validated BLP toolkit. That is a difference in weighting and I do not claim it is decisive.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first and proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues that the Gertler and Gilchrist accelerator strand builds on Bernanke-Gertler work already partly recognised by the 2022 prize, so a two-person award is the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: This changed my view of B006. In my opening I ranked it eighth, partly because of the Bernanke overlap, and I had proposed three names including Gertler. Hassler's two-name framing resolves most of that attribution problem, because Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a clear, self-contained mechanism. It makes B006 a stronger alternative than I credited, which is why I list it. I still ask what the empirical record says about the collateral channel specifically, as opposed to financial frictions in general. If the channel is mainly theoretical validation plus broad model adoption, I would weigh it below a contribution that is both a method and a widely checked empirical practice.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B047 first, and agrees that BLP is the clean core with Pakes's dynamic work adding weight. He ranks B036 second but stresses that its credited list omits Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Yeaple, which weakens the claim of clean attribution.
responses.response: I accept the B036 point and it moves my ordering. I ranked Helpman and Melitz second, but Stromberg and Hassler are right that Melitz built on contemporaneous firm-level work (Bernard-Jensen, Eaton-Kortum) outside the credited names. That makes the credit boundary much less clear than for BLP, where the paper trail points to three people. I keep B036 as an alternative because the contribution is mature and conceptually clean, but I would not put it ahead of B047 on attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer a configuration that recognises the Bresnahan-Reiss empirical-entry tradition or the Benkard-Levin dynamic-estimation line alongside BLP. The three-name limit makes that unresolved.
How much weight to give Pakes's dynamic-oligopoly work relative to the demand-estimation core in the citation.
How far the empirical identification of the collateral channel in B006, and the thematic proximity to the 2022 prize, should lower its standing relative to B047.
My knowledge of citation counts and policy usage comes from general knowledge, not from the supplied evidence, and I have not independently verified it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot. B023 and B031 are near my labour-economics field, so I have applied the same criteria to them as to other fields.
